title: Yunus Emre and Gibb's translation
short: A pantheistic ghazel by the Anatolian Sufi Yunus Emre (d. c. 1320), translated by E. J. W. Gibb in A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (1900).
body: Yunus Emre, a dervish of central Anatolia (c. 1238-1320 by the usual dating), wrote mystical poems in plain Turkish, mostly in the syllabic metres of folk song, which made him one of the founders of Turkish poetry; his poems are still sung in Sufi gatherings. Gibb (1857-1901) printed this ghazel, with notes, in the first volume of his history of the Ottoman poets. Every couplet ends with 'am I', Gibb's rendering of a repeated end-word (redif): the speaker claims to be all things, but the last couplet reveals that the speaker is God's 'Tongue of Power' speaking through Yunus. Editors warn that later poets also signed as 'Yunus', so individual attributions are not always certain.

title: Faith, idol, Ka'ba-fane
greek: Arabic Ka'ba ('cube'); English fane < Latin fanum ('temple')
short: The speaker is at once the true faith, the idol, and the Ka'ba at Mecca: every religion, true and false, is contained in the One.
body: 'Fane' is an archaic poetic word for a temple (OED, fane n.2, from Latin fanum). Gibb explains that the Ka'ba, the 'Cubical House' at Mecca towards which Muslims pray, stands for Islam, and the 'idol' for the other, conventionally false religions: Yunus identifies himself with every form of worship. The pairing of idol and Ka'ba is a commonplace of Persian Sufi poetry (compare Rumi and Hafiz), where the idol-temple and the mosque are equally veils over the one reality. The line is deliberately shocking for orthodox readers, and the poem only justifies it in the final couplet.

title: 'who smites the sphere a-spin'
short: Gibb glosses this as 'He who makes the spheres revolve': the speaker is the mover of the heavens.
body: In the Ptolemaic cosmology shared by Islamic scholars, the heavens are concentric spheres carrying the planets and stars, set in motion by a prime mover. Gibb's note reads the phrase as 'He who makes the spheres revolve'. 'A-spin' is Gibb's archaising coinage on the model of 'a-hunting', meaning 'into spinning'. The same couplet passes from the turning heavens to cloud and rain, so that the speaker is both the highest cause and the humblest weather: Gibb's opening chapter on Ottoman cosmology explains the system of spheres, seas and mountains behind such lines.

title: Thunderbolt and poison-snake
short: The speaker is also the destructive things of creation, lightning and the venomous snake: the One includes what seems evil.
body: The second couplet moves from life-giving rain (couplet 1) to the thunderbolt and the snake that hides in the earth. Pantheistic Sufism, in the tradition associated with Ibn 'Arabi and with Rumi, held that God manifests through both His 'beautiful' and His 'majestic' or terrible attributes, so destruction as well as mercy belongs to the One; Gibb draws on this distinction later in the poem (see 'What coalless burns'). Yunus's catalogue of creatures recalls the many Qur'anic signs (ayat) in nature, but the claim to be them goes beyond the Qur'an's language.

title: Hamza and Mount Qaf
short: Gibb notes an episode in the legendary history of Hamza, the Prophet's uncle, who in popular romance was carried over Qaf, the mountain range at the world's edge.
body: Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, died a martyr at Uhud (625), but a vast popular romance, the Hamzanama, made him a fantastic hero who travels to the lands of the jinn. Gibb's note says only that the line refers to 'an incident in the legendary history of Hamza'. For Qaf he refers to his account of Islamic cosmology: the earth is ringed by the mountains of Qaf and by seas, beyond which dwell the jinn. In this poem the divine speaker claims to be the power that carried the hero across the world's boundary, a mark of the romance's wide popularity.

anchor: who swelled his hands and feet
title: 'who swelled his hands and feet'
short: An obscure detail of the Hamza legend that Gibb does not explain; the sense seems to be that the power made Hamza's limbs grow for his feat.
body: Gibb's note covers the Hamza episode only in general terms, and he leaves 'swelled his hands and feet therewith' without comment; it presumably refers to a detail of the romance in which the hero's body is enlarged to accomplish his superhuman journey, but no source in this archive confirms that, and the phrase should be treated as unexplained. Students should note the limits of Gibb's apparatus here, and that the Hamzanama exists in many versions in Persian and Turkish. The line also illustrates the strain of Gibb's method: he kept the original rhyme and redif, at the cost of filler words like 'therewith'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London: Luzac, 1900), section on Yunus Emre, and notes

title: 'Rayne'
short: An archaic spelling, probably of 'reign' (sovereignty), chosen to rhyme with the poem's '-ain' sounds: 'the King of Wisdom's reign am I'.
body: 'Rayne' is a Middle English and early modern spelling recorded for 'reign' (and also for 'rein' and 'rain'); Gibb gives no note, but the sense 'the King of Wisdom's reign' fits the preceding half-line, 'Who many from their thrones drave off'. Gibb keeps a single rhyme through the ghazal (rain, fain, Rayne, remain, drain, gain, rain, train, I) as the Turkish does, and this odd spelling looks like a deliberately antique choice to distinguish it from the 'rains' of couplet 1. 'Drave' is the archaic past tense of 'drive'.

title: Wisdom's crib and Power's milk
short: The creator who builds bone and flesh is also the infant lying in the cradle and drinking milk: the divine is present at both ends of creation.
body: The couplet moves from God as maker of the body ('Who buildeth bone and flesh and skin') to the image of the speaker as a baby in 'Wisdom's crib' drinking 'Power's milk'. Gibb gives no note; the image seems to make the infant's growth itself a manifestation of divine Wisdom and Power, two of the attributes of God. The capitalised abstractions, Wisdom, Power, Serfhood, are Gibb's way of marking Arabic theological terms in the Turkish (such as hikmet, wisdom, and kudret, power). The language prepares for couplet 6, where God condescends to physical birth.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London: Luzac, 1900), section on Yunus Emre, and notes

title: The heart as God's house
short: Gibb finds 'probably an allusion' to the saying 'the heart of the believer is the house of God'.
body: Gibb points to the Arabic saying 'the heart of the believer is the house of God'; hadith scholars do not accept it as a sound prophetic tradition, but it is everywhere in Sufi writing, together with the related saying in which God declares that neither heaven nor earth can contain Him, but the heart of His believing servant does. 'Repair' here means a place of resort or visiting (OED, repair n.1), so the line says that God makes the human heart His dwelling. The image answers the Ka'ba of couplet 1: the true Ka'ba is the heart.

title: Dam and sire; Serfhood
short: Gibb glosses: He who, while universal, condescends to individual physical birth from mother and father, and knows the worth of servanthood.
body: Gibb's note explains 'consent to dam and sire' as the universal One condescending to individual, physical birth. 'Dam and sire', words normally used of animals, emphasise the bodily nature of that birth. 'Serfhood' renders the condition of being a servant ('abd, Turkish kul) of God, the proper state of the human being in Islamic thought; to 'know Serfhood's gain' is to understand the value of humility and worship. The paradox is that the divine speaker also knows, from the inside, what it is to be a creature who worships.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London: Luzac, 1900), section on Yunus Emre, and notes

title: Light and fire
greek: Arabic nur ('light') and nar ('fire'); jamal and jalal
short: Gibb explains: what burns without coal is Light (nur); what leaps under the hammer is Fire (nar), symbols of God's Beauty and Majesty.
body: Gibb's notes read 'what coalless burns' as Light (nur) and the sparks leaping from iron under the hammer as Fire (nar). In Sufi thought light and fire often stand for the two kinds of divine attributes, the Beautiful (jemal) and the Awful or Majestic (jelal), a distinction Gibb discusses elsewhere in his volume. The smithy image is concrete and Anatolian; the light without fuel recalls the Qur'anic Light Verse (24:35), whose lamp is lit by an oil that 'would well-nigh give light though no fire touched it', a verse Gibb quotes in his note on the next ghazal.

title: 'Time in the Cycle-train'
short: Gibb glosses: 'The circling Time that brings healing on its wings' - the speaker is time itself, turning and restoring.
body: The couplet offers refuge to the sufferer: 'My heart his home, mine eye his town.' Gibb's note glosses 'Time in the Cycle-train' as the circling Time that brings healing on its wings. 'Cycle' is the turning of the heavens (devr), which in Persian and Turkish poetry usually brings misfortune; here it becomes the healing passage of time. 'Train' means a procession or sequence. The compound is typical of Gibb's practice, forcing a Turkish phrase into a hyphenated English one to keep the rhyme.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London: Luzac, 1900), section on Yunus Emre, and notes

title: The signature couplet
short: In the closing couplet, where the poet names himself, Yunus denies authorship: it is not Yunus but the 'Tongue of Power', God, who speaks.
body: Ghazels conventionally name the poet in the last couplet. Yunus uses the convention to resolve the poem's scandal: the 'I' who claimed to be the idol, the Ka'ba and the universe is not the man Yunus but divine Power speaking through him. The idea recalls the Sufi doctrine that the annihilated mystic becomes a mouthpiece of God, and the famous cry of al-Hallaj (executed 922), 'I am the Truth' (ana'l-haqq), which later Sufis defended in just these terms. The 'Tongue of Power' appears again in the next Yunus ghazel in the archive ('Who makes the Tongue of Power to speak').

title: 'paynim' and 'the First and Latest'
short: Whoever disbelieves is a pagan; the speaker is 'the First and the Last', a Qur'anic name of God (57:3).
body: 'Paynim' is an archaic word for a pagan or non-Christian, from Old French paienime (OED, paynim n.); Gibb uses it for the Turkish word for unbeliever. 'The First and the Last' echoes Qur'an 57:3, 'He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward', a verse that Yunus's next ghazel quotes directly ('The Outer and the Inner I, the Former and the Latter I'). The final half-line thus seals the poem's claim with scripture, while the threat to the disbeliever turns the poem's radical claim into a test of faith.
